title: Three Red Panda Cubs Are the Star of This Panda Party
summary:
Happy International Red Panda Day! At the Smithsonian's National Zoo, there are three tiny reasons to celebrate.

Three red panda cubs were born this summer at the zoo's campus in Front Royal, Virginia. On May 29, a mom named Sequoia and dad Mow Mow had twins — one girl, one boy. On June 11, a mom named Keahi had a single girl.

All three are doing well. They've spent the summer in nest boxes, drinking milk and sleeping. They're starting to move around more, and their personalities are showing.

"The singleton... is definitely feisty and huff-quacks at us every chance she gets," said Jessica Kordell, an assistant curator. "The twins are a bit more quiet and shy."

Red pandas are endangered. Fewer than 10,000 live in the wild, in the treetops of Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and China. They eat mostly bamboo — about two to four pounds a day — but can digest only about 24 percent of it. That's why they eat so much!

Their red fur helps them blend in with reddish lichen growing on trees. Their black bellies fade into shadows.

Why does this matter? These cubs pass their parents' genes to the next generation. That helps keep the species going.
why_it_matters: When an animal is endangered, every healthy baby matters — these cubs help make sure red pandas don't disappear from the world you are growing up in.

background_read: International Red Panda Day is celebrated each September to help people learn about these animals.
Red pandas live in the mountain forests of the Himalayas in Asia, and they are not close cousins of giant pandas — they are the only living members of their own animal family.
Zoos around the world join breeding programs to keep red panda families healthy and varied, because the wild population is small and shrinking.
Article_Structure: WHO: Three red panda cubs at the Smithsonian's National Zoo — twins born May 29 and a single girl born June 11 — plus mothers Sequoia and Keahi.
WHAT: The zoo is celebrating the cubs on International Red Panda Day; the cubs are growing, moving around, and showing their personalities.
WHERE: The zoo's campus in Front Royal, Virginia; in the wild, red pandas live in the treetops of Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and China.
WHY: The cubs pass their parents' genes to the next generation, which helps keep the endangered species going.

perspectives.description: They are excited that all three cubs are doing well, and they enjoy watching the twins' shy personalities and the single cub's feisty huff-quacks.
They are glad for the births, but they point out that red pandas in the wild still lose their forest homes, so zoo cubs alone won't save the species.
For families, the cubs are a fun reason to visit the zoo and a chance to learn why some animals need our help.
